sources.text:
Final year group project, Edinburgh, October 2025 to April 2026. We built an internal feature flag service for a local travel booking company that sponsored the project. They wanted to switch features on and off per customer group without redeploying.

We used Go for the API, Postgres for the flag definitions, Redis for the cache the SDKs read from, and we deployed it to their existing Kubernetes cluster with Helm. We wrote SDKs for their two languages, TypeScript and Python.

Our main decision was to push flag changes to the SDKs over server-sent events rather than have the SDKs poll. We chose this because polling every few seconds from a few hundred pods would have hammered the service, and the company wanted changes to show up within a second.

The problem we hit was that under load testing the service fell over at around 300 concurrent SSE connections. We assumed it was Go, but it turned out to be the ingress controller's default connection limits plus a per-pod file descriptor limit. We investigated by comparing the numbers in the ingress logs with what the service itself reported, and we found the service was never even seeing the extra connections. We raised the limits and added a connection count to our Grafana dashboards so we would see it next time. We learned that "the service fell over" is rarely the service's fault alone and you have to look at every hop.

By the end we had it handling 2,000 connections in the load test, and the company put it into a staging environment. We were four people: Aoife, Dan, Priti and me.

Why Graphcore: we visited the Bristol office on a course trip, and the platform work was the part of our project we liked best.
I built the Grafana dashboards and the alert rules, and I ran the load tests that found the connection limit.

sources.text:
Final year group project, Edinburgh, October 2025 to April 2026. We built an internal feature flag service for a local travel booking company that sponsored the project. They wanted to switch features on and off per customer group without redeploying.

We used Go for the API, Postgres for the flag definitions, Redis for the cache the SDKs read from, and we deployed it to their existing Kubernetes cluster with Helm. We wrote SDKs for their two languages, TypeScript and Python.

Our main decision was to push flag changes to the SDKs over server-sent events rather than have the SDKs poll. We chose this because polling every few seconds from a few hundred pods would have hammered the service, and the company wanted changes to show up within a second.

The problem we hit was that under load testing the service fell over at around 300 concurrent SSE connections. We assumed it was Go, but it turned out to be the ingress controller's default connection limits plus a per-pod file descriptor limit. We investigated by comparing the numbers in the ingress logs with what the service itself reported, and we found the service was never even seeing the extra connections. We raised the limits and added a connection count to our Grafana dashboards so we would see it next time. We learned that "the service fell over" is rarely the service's fault alone and you have to look at every hop.

By the end we had it handling 2,000 connections in the load test, and the company put it into a staging environment. We were four people: Aoife, Dan, Priti and me.

Why Graphcore: we visited the Bristol office on a course trip, and the platform work was the part of our project we liked best.

documents.text:
Between October 2025 and April 2026, four of us in Edinburgh built a feature flag service for a local travel booking company that sponsored our final-year project.

We used Go for the API, Postgres for the flag definitions and Redis for the cache that the SDKs read from, and we deployed the service to their existing Kubernetes cluster with Helm. We also wrote SDKs for their two languages, TypeScript and Python.

Our main decision was to push flag changes to the SDKs over server-sent events rather than have the SDKs poll. We chose this because polling every few seconds from a few hundred pods would have hammered the service, and the company wanted changes to show up within a second.

Under load testing, the service fell over at around 300 concurrent SSE connections. We investigated by comparing the numbers in the ingress logs with what the service itself reported, and we found that the service was never even seeing the extra connections. It turned out to be the ingress controller's default connection limits plus a per-pod file descriptor limit, not Go. We raised the limits and added a connection count to our Grafana dashboards so we would see it next time. By the end we had it handling 2,000 connections in the load test, and the company put it into a staging environment. We learned that a failure is rarely the service's fault alone and that every hop must be checked.

We were four people: Aoife, Dan, Priti and me. I built the Grafana dashboards, and Aoife wrote the alert rules. I ran the load tests that found the connection limit.

Dear Graphcore hiring team,

I am applying for the Graduate Cloud Platform Engineer 2027 role at Graphcore.

We visited Graphcore's Bristol office on a course trip, and the platform work was the part of our project we liked best.

We built an internal feature flag service for a local travel booking company that sponsored the project. They wanted to switch features on and off per customer group without redeploying. We used Go, Postgres, Redis, Kubernetes and Helm for the service. We wrote SDKs for TypeScript and Python. We decided to push flag changes over server-sent events rather than have SDKs poll. We chose this because polling would have hammered the service and changes were wanted within a second.

I ran the load tests that found the connection limit. Under load testing, the service fell over at around 300 concurrent SSE connections. We investigated by comparing ingress logs with service reports and found extra connections never reached the service. The cause was ingress controller connection limits plus a per-pod file descriptor limit, not Go. I built the Grafana dashboards, and Aoife wrote the alert rules. We raised the limits and added a connection count to Grafana dashboards. By the end we had it handling 2,000 connections and the company put it into staging. We learned a failure is rarely the service's fault alone and every hop must be checked.

Thank you for considering my application.

Kind regards,
